# Introduction

**Electroencephalography (EEG)** is widely utilized for its unparalleled temporal resolution, which allows researchers to study neural dynamics _in vivo_. However, as measurements are primarily recorded at the scalp, the technique suffers from poor spatial resolution. In 1993, the **Minimum Norm Estimate (MNE)** was introduced to project EEG data onto a cortical surface modeled from individual MRI [@dale_improved_1993]. This approach, broadly termed **source reconstruction**, aimed to combine the high temporal resolution of EEG with the spatial precision of structural imaging.

Despite three decades of evolution into a diverse array of variants (e.g., sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002], eLORETA [@pascual-marqui_discrete_2007], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], LCMV [@van_veen_localization_1997]), these methods are still primarily used to identify isolated brain regions — a practice often called **source localization** [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. This focus on localization overlooks a fundamental shift in modern neuroscience toward **connectomics**. As the "localizationist" view reaches its theoretical limits, it is being superseded by **connectivity neuroscience**, which treats the brain as an integrated system of interacting networks rather than a collection of independent regions [@bressler_large-scale_2010].

Widely used source reconstruction methods — such as sLORETA, eLORETA, dSPM, and LCMV — remain largely ill-suited for this shift because they rely on the assumption of **independent sources**, a prior known to perform worse than one informed by the true source covariance structure [@wipf_unified_2009]. This assumption is defensible when activity is genuinely focal — for example, identifying the cortical onset of a sensory stimulus or an epileptic spike — but breaks down as soon as multiple brain regions are simultaneously involved. Because the EEG inverse problem is fundamentally ill-posed due to volume conduction, reconstructed activity from interacting sources blurs together across the cortex, a phenomenon known as **leakage** [@schoffelen_source_2009]. A structured prior on source interactions cannot remove this ill-posedness, but, unlike the independent-sources assumption, it can mitigate leakage's impact [@gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018].

Several strategies have been proposed to address this. Some methods incorporate functional priors from fMRI to constrain expected source interactions [@liu_fmri-si-stbf_2021]; however, this approach is constrained by the mismatch between fMRI's hemodynamic response, which unfolds over seconds, and the millisecond-scale dynamics of EEG source activity, limiting how precisely such a prior can constrain the interactions it is meant to inform. Others take an agnostic approach, jointly estimating source activities and their unknown covariance structure from the data itself — a family exemplified by **BC-VARETA** [@gonzalez-moreira_third_2018], at the cost of greater ill-posedness and computational expense. A third strategy draws on the growing body of evidence for **structure–function coupling**: since neural activity is known to propagate along the brain's structural scaffolding, the connectome estimated from diffusion MRI tractography provides a principled and subject-specific prior for source reconstruction [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024].

**Graph Signal Processing (GSP)** provides the mathematical machinery to exploit this coupling [@shuman_emerging_2013]. By applying eigendecomposition to the connectome's graph Laplacian, one obtains an orthonormal set of **brain harmonics** — eigenvectors ordered by their associated graph frequency [@atasoy_human_2016]. Low-frequency harmonics capture smooth, globally integrated patterns of activity; high-frequency harmonics encode more locally segregated ones. Projecting source activity onto this eigenbasis — the **Graph Fourier Transform (GFT)** — yields a compact representation termed the **connectome spectrum**. Crucially, recent work has demonstrated that both fMRI and EEG source activity are highly compact in this domain: activity energy concentrates predominantly in low-frequency harmonics and decays following an inverse curve, reflecting the tendency of brain dynamics to align with the smooth, integrative modes of the structural connectome [@atasoy_human_2016; @rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. **Rué-Queralt et al. (2024)** leveraged this principle to introduce **Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET)**: a source reconstruction method that enforces an L₁ sparsity prior directly in the connectome spectrum, restricting solutions to a small number of active harmonics and thereby embedding structural organisation into the reconstruction.

Similar concepts have been explored using the **Beltrami-Laplace operator** applied to the cortical mesh rather than the connectome's graph Laplacian [@pang_geometric_2023]. This substitutes white matter tractography with the local geometry of the gray matter surface, capturing fine-grained short-range connectivity at the expense of the long-range structural pathways defined by white matter tracts. **Pang et al. (2023)** showed that geometric eigenmodes derived this way reconstruct functional brain activity at least as accurately as eigenmodes derived from structural connectomes, indicating that cortical geometry alone can yield spectral representations of neural signals that are comparably compact to connectome-based ones [@pang_geometric_2023]. Building on this, **Wang et al. (2026)** developed **Geometric Basis Functions (GBF)**, representing whole-brain EEG/MEG activity as a linear combination of the leading ~200 Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical surface (capturing ~87% of cortical variance), regularized by an L₂ penalty whose weight decays exponentially across eigenvalue-ordered geometric modes [@wang_geometry_2026]. **Pok Him Siu et al.**, by contrast, proposed a weighted spectral method based on SVD truncation of the forward operator: the weighted Beltrami-operator harmonics act as a hard spectral filter applied after source reconstruction — determining which components are retained — rather than as a continuous penalty embedded in the optimization itself [@siu_structural_2026].

So far, CSET has no principled way to distinguish biologically meaningful harmonics from those dominated by noise, unlike the geometry-based methods described above, which weight low-order harmonics preferentially by construction. In this work, we address this with weighted CSET (wCSET), which replaces the L₁ prior with a weighted L₂ prior whose penalties follow an exponential decay on graph frequency — resembling GBF's continuous, eigenvalue-graded penalty, but applied to the connectome's graph Laplacian rather than the cortical mesh's Beltrami-Laplace operator. Such a weighting is well justified by the findings of **Abdelnour et al. (2018)** [@abdelnour_functional_2018], who show that functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural connectome Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, so that a small number of low-frequency structural eigenmodes dominate functional connectivity — consistent with the broader tendency of brain signal energy to concentrate in, and decay across, low graph frequencies [@huang_graph_2016]. Unlike the geometry-based approaches described above, the graph used here is a connectome that is fully aware of the underlying white matter tracts.

Despite this progression from a fixed L₁ sparsity prior to increasingly principled, geometry- and connectome-informed spectral weightings, a critical gap remains in how these methods have actually been validated. **Rué-Queralt et al.** validated CSET by correlating reconstructed source activity with fMRI data from the same task. Yet fMRI measures hemodynamic responses — blood oxygenation changes driven by neurovascular coupling — which reflect neural activity only indirectly and with significant temporal blurring. The resulting mismatch between EEG source reconstructions and fMRI extends well beyond what correlation can account for, and constitutes a weak proxy for the electrophysiological ground truth these methods aim to reconstruct. The remaining works validate through source localization in epilepsy patients. While some report improvements in estimated source extent, this evaluation criterion is misaligned with the aim of connectivity-informed methods, which are designed not to refine the spatial footprint of a focal source, but to capture the dynamics of activity across interconnected networks — a capability that localization accuracy does not measure.

The primary barrier to a more appropriate validation is therefore the lack of a **ground truth for interconnected neural dynamics**. We address this gap on two complementary fronts. First, we simulate activity propagating across the structural connectome itself (Section 2.1.1), which provides an exact, fully known ground truth for network-level dynamics that no empirical recording can offer. Second, we revive and extend the framework proposed by **Grova et al. (2016)** [@grova_intracranial_2016], who correlated MEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings from the same patients — extending it here to truly simultaneous EEG and iEEG recordings. Unlike fMRI or localization benchmarks, iEEG directly measures electrical potential within the brain — free from neurovascular coupling, skull attenuation, and temporal blurring — making it the only available electrophysiological ground truth for dynamic source reconstruction. By projecting EEG-reconstructed sources onto iEEG electrode locations, we obtain two directly comparable datasets — **estimated iEEG** and **true iEEG** — providing an electrophysiologically grounded benchmark for evaluating source reconstruction beyond localization.

We utilize this framework alongside a clinical localization cohort to evaluate **CSET** and **wCSET** across three complementary studies:

- **Study I:** Using simulations of spontaneous source diffusion via dMRI-based structural connectivity, we demonstrate that while standard methods accurately localize a source's _onset_, connectivity-informed methods are significantly superior at capturing its _propagation_. We also assess the robustness of these methods against dataerroneous connectivity data.

- **Study II:** Using a clinical epilepsy dataset where post-surgical success defines the ground truth, we show that connectivity-informed methods preserve localization accuracy comparable to gold-standard clinical algorithms — confirming that the gain in network sensitivity does not come at the cost of focal precision.

- **Study III:** Using simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings, we validate source reconstruction directly against intracranial measurements, demonstrating the ability of connectivity-informed methods to map dynamic neural networks beyond simple point-source localization.

Together, these studies establish wCSET as a principled and clinically viable tool for reconstructing distributed brain dynamics, and introduce a multi-level validation framework that moves the field beyond localization as the sole benchmark for source imaging.

## Data Acquisition and Datasets1

### Synthetic Data

Simulations were conducted using anatomical data from a single representative subject selected from the VEPCON dataset [@pascucci_source_2022]. The anatomical framework consists of a T1-weighted MRI and a corresponding structural tractogram derived from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). EEG signals were simulated on a 204-channel montage derived from a 256-channel EGI HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net, after removing cheek electrodes. The cortical source space (Section 2.3.1) was parcellated into brain regions using the MultiConn atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022] (~400 regions, 2–10 dipoles per region). To keep the simulation budget tractable while retaining broad cortical coverage, a subset of 100 regions was selected via greedy farthest-point sampling over region centroids, yielding a spatially uniform probe set that is reused across every simulation-based analysis in this study except the noise-robustness analysis (Section 3.1.2): sweeping multiple SNR levels per region across the full 100-region set would have been computationally impractical, so a separate, independently-sampled subset of 50 regions was used there instead. In each simulation trial, a source region was drawn from the relevant probe set, and a spike-like waveform was assigned to all dipoles within that region, following classic simulation approaches in which epileptiform activity is modelled as a patch of simultaneously active dipoles rather than a single point source [@afnan_eegmeg_2024]. The spike waveform is a double Hanning window defined as:

$$
s_0(t) = \begin{cases} h\!\left(t,\, \tfrac{2}{3}W\right) & 0 \leq t \leq \tfrac{2}{3}W \\[4pt] -\tfrac{1}{2}\,h\!\left(t - \tfrac{2}{3}W,\; \tfrac{1}{3}W\right) & \tfrac{2}{3}W < t \leq W \end{cases}
$$

where $h(t, T) = \frac{1}{2}\!\left[1 - \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right)\right]$ is a Hanning window of duration $T$, and $W = 0.05$ s (50 ms) is the total spike duration, chosen to fall centrally within the consensus clinical EEG duration convention for interictal spikes specifically (20–70 ms) [@kane_revised_2017]. The waveform consists of a dominant positive lobe spanning two-thirds of the spike duration, followed by a half-amplitude negative rebound over the remaining third, mimicking the morphology of a clinical interictal spike <!-- supp fig (spike example)-->. The spike signal is then convolved with a Dirac comb recurring every 1 s into a 20 s simulated recording, to generate a train of 20 spike events at the source level; once propagated across the connectome and projected to the sensors (see below and Section 2.2), these are epoched around each event and averaged in EEG sensor space into a single evoked response per simulated run, mirroring the spike-triggered averaging used to construct the clinical datasets in Studies 2 and 3.
**Propagation model.** Activity was propagated across the connectome in a feedforward manner. The activity at dipole $j$ was modelled as:

$$
S_j(t) = \gamma^{h_j} \cdot s_0\!\left(t - \tau_j\right)
$$

where $s_0(t)$ is the source waveform, $h_j$ is the number of hops (graph edges) along the shortest path from the source to dipole $j$, and $\gamma \in [0,1]$ is a per-hop spatial decay factor, set to $\gamma = 0.5$: without it, activity would propagate undiminished along every reachable path and spread across the entire connectome, rather than attenuating with network distance from the source as genuine, spatially-bounded propagation should. The total propagation delay $\tau_j$ was computed as the sum of per-edge delays along that path:

$$
\tau_j = \sum_{(u,v)\,\in\,\mathcal{P}_j} \!\left(\frac{l_{uv}}{v(l_{uv})} + \tau_p\right) + \epsilon_\tau, \qquad v(l) = \begin{cases} 4.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l > 35 \text{ mm (long-range)} \\ 2.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l \leq 35 \text{ mm (U-fiber)} \end{cases}
$$

where $l_{uv}$ is the fiber length of edge $(u,v)$ in mm, and $v(l_{uv})$ is a conduction speed that depends on fiber length: 4.5 mm/ms for long-range tracts above 35 mm — the central estimate of two independent large-sample cortico-cortical evoked potential (CCEP) studies converging on ~3–6 m/s for adult long-range association fibers [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023] — and a slower 2.5 mm/ms for short-range U-fibers at or below 35 mm, reflecting their distinctly slower reported conduction (~2–3 m/s) relative to long-range tracts [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023]. $\tau_p = 7$ ms is a fixed nodal delay per hop representing synaptic transmission plus relay latency, matching the population-level synaptic time constants estimated directly from CCEP modelling [@lemarechal_brain_2022]. $\epsilon_\tau \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\tau)$, with $\sigma_\tau = 1$ ms, is a per-dipole jitter term modelling uncertainty in propagation timing, accumulated once per hop along the shortest path (i.e. scaling with $\sqrt{h_j}$ rather than a single flat perturbation of the total path delay). <!-- supp fig (propagation video)-->

**Noise model.** Pink noise was added at the source level to model background neural activity, and independent white noise was added at the sensor level to model measurement noise. Sensor-level noise comprised a small fixed instrument/electrode-noise floor (2.0 µV RMS) plus a source-space contribution solved, for each head model, to bring the total delivered sensor-level baseline noise to a target of 15.0 µV RMS — the literature midpoint of the commonly-cited ~10–20 µV RMS scalp EEG background noise range [@nunez_electric_2006]. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was calibrated to a fixed single-trial target of 5 (peak amplitude relative to baseline standard deviation) by scaling the source activity prior to sensor projection: this sits above the ~2.0–3.2 linear-ratio range reported for single-trial interictal spikes [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024], chosen as a practical compromise to keep delivered spikes comfortably above the simulator's own noise floor while remaining much closer to the single-trial literature range than a post-averaging-scale target would be. All parameters are summarised in @tbl-sim-params.

Each simulation was repeated 8 times per source region. The number of regions and repetitions were set via a power analysis <!-- supp fig (power analysis, simf --> targeting adequate power for the region-paired method comparisons reported throughout the Results — i.e., ensuring that the relative ranking of reconstruction methods is robust across a spatially-diverse sample of source regions rather than reflecting any single one (the main effect of method alone was already saturated at power ≈ 1.0 across every tested design).

### Clinical Dataset A — Resection Cohort

To validate electroencephalographic source imaging clinically, we used the dataset of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025, comprising 44 patients with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy who underwent resective surgery. Surgical outcome was assessed at 12 months post-operatively and graded on the ILAE scale (1 = seizure-free, 2–6 = increasing degrees of persistent seizures). We restricted analysis to patients with a seizure-free outcome (ILAE 1), yielding 28 patients: for patients with residual seizures, the resection may not have fully encompassed the true epileptogenic zone, making the resected volume an unreliable ground truth for localization accuracy in that group. Resection masks were obtained as described in Section 2.5.1. Two further patients were excluded from the seizure-free subset: one had no genuine resection cavity for any candidate mask to capture, and the other was missing usable EEG channel locations for coregistration — yielding a final cohort of 26 patients. Each patient's data consisted of a pre-operative T1-weighted MRI and a pre-operative interictal EEG recording, as well as a post-operative T1-weighted MRI. The dataset provides 257-channel high-density EEG (HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net); cheek electrodes were excluded, yielding the 204-channel montage used throughout this study. Interictal epileptic discharges had been visually identified by clinical experts among the dataset's authors and were time-locked averaged at their peak.

Individual diffusion MRI was not available for this cohort, so the structural connectome was derived from the population probabilistic tractography atlas (Section 2.3.3) rather than subject-specific tractography.

## Signal Preprocessing


### EEG/iEEG Processing

**Studies 1 and 3 (Simulation and Simultaneous EEG/iEEG).** EEG data were available as epochs time-locked to the interictal spike peak — the known peak of the simulated source event in Study 1, and the peak of the simultaneously recorded intracranial (iEEG) signal in Study 3, rather than a peak independently detected on the scalp EEG itself. A Common Average Reference (CAR) was applied, consistent with standard practice for source reconstruction [@bertrand_theoretical_1985]. Baseline correction was performed using the pre-spike period, and an empirical noise covariance matrix was estimated from the same baseline window for subsequent data whitening. Epochs were then averaged to obtain the evoked response: exactly 20 spike epochs per simulated run in Study 1 (Section 2.1.1), and a variable number of clinically marked interictal spikes per subject in Study 3 (130–265 across the four subjects). For the Study 3 channel-comparison analysis (Section 2.6.3), the analysis window around each spike was defined by thresholding the global field power (GFP) of the evoked response: the continuous interval around the peak over which GFP stays above 3 standard deviations of the pre-spike baseline, rather than the fixed handful of samples around the peak used by @grova_intracranial_2016.

**Study 2 (Clinical Dataset A — resection cohort).** EEG data were provided as pre-averaged interictal discharge waveforms; individual epochs were not available. Preprocessing by the data providers included bandpass filtering (high-pass: 0.3–1 Hz; low-pass: 30–100 Hz, with filter settings varying across patients due to the longitudinal nature of the dataset), downsampling to 250 Hz, and interpolation of noisy channels from neighbouring electrodes using 3D splines. Since individual epochs were unavailable, noise covariance estimation and data whitening were not performed. A Common Average Reference was applied. A subset of subjects presented residual 50 Hz line noise and required an additional notch filter. Baseline correction was applied to subjects whose recordings lacked it.

**iEEG (Study 3).** Intracranial recordings were available as epochs time-locked to the spike peak. Epochs were averaged directly to obtain the ground-truth intracranial evoked response; no further preprocessing was applied.

## Forward Modeling and Structural Priors

### Source Space

We modeled neural activity using a distributed dipole model with a cortical constraint. The source space was restricted to the cortical white matter surface, reconstructed from T1-weighted MRI data using FreeSurfer (v7.4.1). Approximately 7,600 dipoles (oct6 icosahedral subdivision, after excluding medial-wall and non-cortical vertices) were uniformly distributed across this surface using MNE-Python (v1.9.0; @gramfort_meg_2013), at an average inter-dipole spacing of approximately 3.3 mm, with dipole orientations fixed normal to the cortical manifold — a constraint widely adopted in distributed source imaging because the dominant contributors to the EEG signal, pyramidal neurons, have net dipole moments oriented normal to the cortical surface [@dale_improved_1993].

### Volume Conduction Model

The forward problem involves calculating the electrical potential at the sensor locations generated by unitary dipole activity within the source space. To model the volume conduction between the sources and sensors, we employed a Boundary Element Model (BEM) [@hamalainen_realistic_1989]. A standard BEM represents the interfaces between major head tissues—specifically the inner skull, outer skull, and outer skin—assuming homogeneous and isotropic electrical conductivity within each compartment. We used the MNE-Python default conductivity values of 0.3 S/m for the brain and scalp, and 0.006 S/m for the skull. While MNE-Python typically relies on FreeSurfer's watershed algorithm for surface extraction, this approach often yields sub-optimal geometries for BEM. To improve the accuracy of the head model, we implemented a custom pipeline: brain tissues were segmented into three compartments (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) using the SimNIBS CHARM pipeline (v4.5; @puonti_accurate_2020). Each compartment mask was smoothed via morphological closing and fitted with a deformable grade-5 icosahedral template. The three surfaces were fitted sequentially — inner skull first, then outer skull, then scalp — with each surface constrained to lie outside the previous one, ensuring non-intersecting layers <!-- supp fig (BEM models)-->.

Since the EEG sensors were pre-co-registered to the T1-weighted MRI, they were intrinsically aligned with the resulting head model. The final forward solution (the gain matrix) was computed using MNE-Python. This forward solution was used across all three studies.

For Study 1 only, a second forward solution was computed for source reconstruction, with the skull conductivity increased to 0.012 S/m while keeping brain and scalp conductivities unchanged at 0.3 S/m. This deliberate mismatch avoids the inverse crime [@wirgin_inverse_2004] — the circularity that arises when the same head model is used for both generating and inverting simulated data, which artificially inflates reconstruction accuracy. A similar strategy — perturbing skull conductivity between the forward and inverse models to avoid this circularity — has been used elsewhere to probe the sensitivity of EEG source analysis to head-model mismatch [@vorwerk_skull_2014]. The two forward models differ by approximately 10% <!-- supp fig (Head model differences)-->.

### Connectivity Matrices

In this work, the brain is modeled as a graph (or connectome) where nodes represent localized brain regions - specifically dipoles in our source space - and edges represent the structural scaffolding between them. For the Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) source reconstruction method and its weighted version (wCSET), we utilize a structural connectome, where edges represent physical anatomical links.

**Empirical connectomes**

We incorporate two distinct types of structural links:
1. Long-range connections: These represent white matter tracts (axonal bundles) estimated via diffusion MRI (dMRI) tractography.
2. Short-range connections: To account for local gray matter connectivity not captured by standard tractography, we connect each dipole to its geodesically nearest neighbors on the cortical manifold, subject to two constraints: a maximum geodesic distance of 15 mm, and a maximum of 8 such neighbors per dipole.

To ensure physical consistency, edges are weighted by distance (in mm): fiber length for long-range tracts and geodesic distance for local connections.

**Connectome surrogates**

In clinical settings where diffusion data may be unavailable, we evaluate three connectome surrogates validated through our simulation framework (see Section 3.1). Two of these are also tested in a binarized form (edge presence only, discarding distance weights) to separate the contribution of connectome topology from that of edge-weight fidelity — the Beltrami-operator surrogate has no such counterpart (see below) — five surrogate variants in total:
- Fused (sparse) atlas surrogate: Long-range tracts are extrapolated from the MultiConn atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], built from a reference population of 66 subjects. We parcellate the subject's brain according to the atlas and identify region pairs connected by a tract present across all 66 subjects in the reference population. Instead of connecting every dipole pair between two such atlas-connected regions, only a fraction of the possible dipole-to-dipole edges is instantiated, at a sparsity level (14%) that we determined by matching the edge density of the single subject in our sample for whom an empirical structural connectome was available. Gray matter connections are then added as described above.
- Geometry-only surrogate: This model relies solely on gray matter connectivity derived from the brain mesh, with nodes additionally connected across hemispheres to their homotopic (mirror-symmetric) partner to keep the resulting graph connected. While distinct from the Beltrami-operator geometry below, this surrogate tests the hypothesis that local brain geometry alone can capture significant brain-function coupling without explicit long-range information.
- Beltrami-operator surrogate: Eigenmodes are computed directly from the Laplace-Beltrami operator applied to the cortical mesh of each hemisphere, using the `lapy` Python library for the underlying finite-element stiffness/mass matrix assembly, without ever constructing an explicit dipole-to-dipole connectome. This mesh is the triangulation of the source space itself, in dipole space (Section 2.3.1) — the decimated, cortex-only surface used for the dipoles — rather than the dense FreeSurfer surface typically used for this computation [@pang_geometric_2023].<!-- Mention that we are doing the same thing as in the gbf paper. --> This is the purest geometry-only control: unlike the geometry-only surrogate above, it does not threshold or weight a graph of geodesic distances at all, so there is no meaningful binarized counterpart to test.

**Connectome perturbation**
 
In the simulation, one has access to the exact connectome used to generate the data; in reality, one never has this exact knowledge. To evaluate robustness to this mismatch, we implemented a procedure to perturb the connectome before applying source reconstruction (see Section 3.1.2): a degree-preserving double-edge swap, in which two existing edges are picked at random and their endpoints re-paired to form two new edges, so that each node's total number of connections is left unchanged.

Perturbation severity is expressed as a percentage of the connectome's total edge count, ranging from 0% (the original, unperturbed connectome) to 100%, at which point as good as none of the original edges remain.

**Graph Fourier Transform**
The connectome edges described above are weighted by the element-wise inverse of their distances (fiber length for long-range tracts, geodesic distance for short-range links), so that spatially closer, more direct structural connections receive proportionally larger weight than distant ones — the natural convention for a graph meant to capture how strongly two dipoles are structurally coupled, since raw distance alone would otherwise assign the largest values to the weakest, most indirect links. These inverse-distance weights populate the connectome's adjacency matrix A, from which we compute the graph Laplacian L = D − A (where D is the degree matrix) — the representation that allows us to apply the tools of Graph Signal Processing (GSP) to neural data [@shuman_emerging_2013; @ortega_graph_2018].

Just as the classical Fourier Transform decomposes a time-series into sine and cosine waves, the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) decomposes brain activity into a set of graph harmonics. These harmonics are the eigenvectors $u_k$ of the Graph Laplacian, obtained via the eigendecomposition: 
$$
\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top
$$

where $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ contains the eigenvalues (graph frequencies) and $\mathbf{U} = [u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_N]$ forms the orthonormal eigenbasis.


## Source Reconstruction Framework

For every study, we used MNE-Python's widely used methods wMNE [@dale_improved_1993], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000] and sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002] (see Section 2.4.1), and compare these to three connectivity-informed methods CSET, wCSET and GBF (see Section 2.4.2). All methods used data whitening based on an empirically estimated noise covariance matrix — a standard preprocessing step in linear M/EEG source reconstruction that decorrelates and normalizes sensor noise before inversion [@dale_dynamic_2000; @knosche_eegmeg_2022] — with one exception: for the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A), the data were provided as pre-averaged discharges with no accompanying baseline epochs, so no empirical noise covariance could be computed, and an ad-hoc (identity-like) covariance was used instead, i.e. no whitening.

### Standard Inverse Solutions

In the M/EEG inverse problem, we aim to estimate underlying dipole activities $\mathbf s\in \mathbb R^n$ from observed sensor measurements $\mathbf y \in \mathbb R^m$. This relationship is defined by the forward model:

$$
\mathbf y = \mathbf L \mathbf s + \epsilon
$$

where $\mathbf L$ is the lead-field matrix and $\epsilon$ represents additive noise. Because the number of dipoles greatly exceeds the number of sensors ($n\gg m$), the problem is ill-posed and lacks a unique solution without further constraints.

From a Bayesian perspective, $\mathbf s$ is treated as a random variable with a prior distribution $P(\mathbf s)$ [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Assuming a Gaussian prior $\mathbf s \sim \mathcal N(0, \Sigma_{\mathbf s})$, reconstruction becomes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation, leading to the optimization problem:
$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\underbrace{\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2}_{\text{Data Fidelity}} + \lambda\underbrace{\lVert \mathbf C \mathbf s\rVert_p^p}_{\text{Regularization}} \tag{1}
$$

Here, $\lambda$ is the regularization parameter balancing data fit with prior assumptions. The matrix $\mathbf C$ acts as a weighting matrix derived from the prior covariance, such that $\mathbf C^T\mathbf C = \mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1}$. In practice, the true source covariance $\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ is unknown and replaced with the identity matrix — the assumption of independent, equal-variance sources that gives wMNE, dSPM and sLORETA their "independent-source" label throughout this work.

wMNE additionaly ajusts source variances generating the depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ applied to counteract the bias of $l_2$-regularized solutions toward superficial dipoles:

$$
\mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1} = \mathbf W_d, \qquad \text{where} \quad W_{d,ii} = \lVert \mathbf L_{:i}\rVert^{-\kappa}
$$

For wMNE, the depth-weighting exponent was set to the standard literature value of $\kappa=0.8$ [@lin_assessing_2006]. sLORETA and dSPM apply an additional post-hoc standardization on top of the minimum-norm estimate, and were run without additional depth weighting, since this noise-normalization step already compensates for depth bias on its own.

While it is widely accepted that source activity is heavily interdependent, these independent-source assumptions are typically chosen because estimating source co-dependence has remained computationally or theoretically elusive. The methods introduced next address this gap directly, by embedding structural connectivity into the source-covariance prior itself.

### Connectivity-Informed Inverse Solution

This section describes the three connectivity-informed inverse solutions compared throughout this work, introduced in order: CSET [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024], the connectome-spectrum $l_1$ sparsity prior our approach builds on; weighted CSET (wCSET), this work's central methodological contribution, which replaces CSET's $l_1$ prior with a smooth, harmonic-weighted $l_2$ prior over the connectome spectrum; and GBF [@wang_geometry_2026], a geometry-based method that shares wCSET's smooth $l_2$ formulation but operates on the eigenbasis of cortical geometry rather than the connectome.

**Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography**

Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024] addresses the independence limitation, by operating in a component-based space. Instead of solving for activity in the brain's physical space, CSET projects the activity onto the eigenmodes of the connectome ($\mathbf U$). This transforms the problem into the "connectome spectrum" space, where the prior can be more effectively described. As with wMNE, CSET and wCSET first counteract the bias toward superficial dipoles with the same depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ (defined above), applied directly to the lead field prior to projection onto the eigenbasis; unlike wMNE's literature-standard $\kappa=0.8$, CSET and wCSET use $\kappa=0.2$, tuned against reconstruction accuracy in the simulation study (Section 3.1).

Given that the connectome spectrum is known to be compact, CSET enforces sparsity by applying an $l_1$​-norm to the regularizer. Let $\mathbf {\hat s}$ represent the spectrum of $\mathbf s$ (where $\mathbf s = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}$). Equation (1) is then modified to: 
$$
\mathbf {\hat s}^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_1 \tag{2}
$$

The physical brain activity is then recovered via $\mathbf s^* = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf{\hat s}^*$.

**weighted CSET**

While basic CSET enforces sparsity, it does not necessarily distinguish between signal and noise in a physiologically informed way. We address this with weighted CSET (wCSET), which replaces CSET's $l_1$ sparsity prior with a smooth, weighted $l_2$ prior over the connectome spectrum. Harmonic weights follow an exponential low-pass filter on graph frequency, $W_{h,ii} = \exp(-\beta\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ is harmonic $i$'s eigenvalue and $\beta$ controls the filter's decay rate, tuned against this connectome's own reconstruction accuracy. This form remains compact since the signal is compressed in the low frequencies and is motivated by the structure–function coupling literature: functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, i.e. a small number of low-frequency structural harmonics dominate functional coupling [@abdelnour_functional_2018]. Equation (2) thus becomes:

$$
\mathbf {\hat s}^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf W_h\mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 \tag{3}
$$

where $\mathbf W_h$ is the diagonal matrix of harmonic weights above. Unlike CSET's $l_1$ sparsity prior, which selects a small number of active harmonics, wCSET's $l_2$ prior smoothly downweights high-frequency harmonics while leaving the low-frequency end of the spectrum comparatively unpenalized. The physical brain activity is again recovered via $\mathbf s^* = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf{\hat s}^*$.

Neither CSET nor wCSET is tied to a particular way of building the connectome that defines $\mathbf U$. What the framework requires is a structural graph whose edges reflect the strength of information flow between dipoles; how that graph is estimated (dMRI tractography, as used here, or an alternative that forgoes an explicit graph altogether, such as the Laplace-Beltrami operator applied to the cortical mesh, Section 2.3.3) and how its edges are weighted (inverse geodesic/fiber distance, as used here, but equally fiber count or raw fiber length) are choices external to the formalism itself. The specific connectome construction adopted in this work (Section 2.3.3) is one principled instantiation, motivated by the structure–function coupling literature [@abdelnour_functional_2018].

**Geometric Basis Functions**

As a further reference method, we reconfigure wCSET (Eq. 3) to reproduce **Wang et al. (2026)**'s Geometric Basis Functions (GBF) [@wang_geometry_2026] as closely as our framework allows, rather than reimplementing their exact pipeline — mesh resolution and regularization differ. Three changes distinguish this GBF-like variant from the connectome-based wCSET above: (i) the connectome eigenbasis $\mathbf U$ is replaced by the eigenvectors of the Laplace-Beltrami operator applied to the cortical mesh (Section 2.3.3), so the spectral decomposition reflects cortical geometry rather than white-matter connectivity; (ii) no depth weighting is applied ($\mathbf W_d = \mathbf I$), matching GBF's original formulation, which includes no depth term; and (iii) wCSET's smooth exponential harmonic weights (Eq. 3) are replaced by GBF's log-form weighting, $W_{h,ii} = \sqrt{-\log(\mu_i/\mu_S)}$ for the $S$ lowest-frequency Beltrami eigenmodes and $W_{h,ii}=0$ beyond, where $\mu_i$ denotes the Laplace-Beltrami operator's eigenvalues (as opposed to the connectome graph Laplacian's $\lambda_i$ used in Eq. 3). This weighting differs from wCSET's in two independent ways: the truncation is hard rather than smoothly decaying, and its log-form shape was selected by Wang et al. on empirical grounds, unlike wCSET's exponential form, which follows directly from the structure–function coupling rationale of Eq. 3 [@abdelnour_functional_2018]. We set $S=150$, tuned against reconstruction accuracy in the simulation study (Section 3.1), rather than the $S=300$ used in the original GBF publication: Wang et al. tune a scale parameter $\beta$ for their log-form weighting, but our pipeline trace-renormalizes the inverse kernel before the ridge solve (standard practice), which renders $\beta$ a pure rescale with no effect on the reconstruction. Rather than leave this comparator's one nominally free parameter untuned, we instead tuned the parameter that actually shapes the weighting under our normalization, the cutoff $S$: a sweep against simulated ground truth showed $S=150$ roughly halving peak-localization error relative to $S=300$ (6.1 vs. 14.7 mm) while matching or exceeding it on average precision. This geometry-only comparator, in the spirit of GBF and related cortical-geometry approaches [@pang_geometric_2023; @wang_geometry_2026; @siu_structural_2026] (Section 1), is tested as a connectome surrogate in the simulation study (Section 3.1.4), and included as a full fourth reference method in the two clinical studies (Sections 3.2, 3.3).

## Clinical Ground Truth Definition

In contrast to the simulated framework, we usually do not have the exact brain activity maps to evaluate source reconstruction methods. We therefore use proxies which allow us to test specific aspects of the method. In the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A; Section 2.1.2), we use the fact that patients underwent surgery, had a brain section removed, and were symptom-free of epilepsy after the surgery. We use the resected area as ground truth to measure the source localization error. We therefore need to segment the resected area (see Section 2.5.1). In the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Clinical Dataset B; Section 2.1.3), we have the recordings of electric potential inside the brain, but only in a few areas. For that, we need to estimate the underlying potential generated by our reconstructed maps (which show dipole currents) at the same locations as the intracranial channels. We use for that a simplified version of the forward problem (see Section 2.5.2).

### Resected Area Segmentation

This section applies to the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A; Section 2.1.2). Resection masks were generated using RAMPS [@simpson_automated_2025], an automated segmentation-and-registration pipeline that estimates the resected volume directly from a subject's pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI. RAMPS additionally requires the hemisphere of the resection and the resected lobe (temporal, frontal, parietal, occipital, or a combination thereof) as input: the lobe was unambiguous from the clinical record for temporal resections, and was determined by visual comparison of the pre- and post-operative images for extratemporal resections. Resulting masks underwent visual quality review by overlaying the pre-operative T1w, post-operative T1w, and resection mask, and were replaced with a manually-segmented mask for a minority of patients whose automated mask was unusable on this review or for whom RAMPS could not be run; subjects whose mask remained missing, incomplete, or clearly incorrect after this process were excluded (Section 2.1.2).

### Source-to-iEEG Projection

This section applies to the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Clinical Dataset B; Section 2.1.3). Following source reconstruction, the estimated cortical activity was projected onto the coordinates of the intracranial electrodes to generate "virtual" iEEG potentials. This projection followed the methodology of **Grova et al. (2016)**. Given that this step assumes the sources and sensors reside within the same compartment, we modeled this as an infinite homogeneous conduction problem. The potential $\Phi$ at a location $r$ is estimated from the brain activity as:
$$
\Phi(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3}
$$

Following the adjustments proposed by **Cosandier-Rimélé et al. (2007)** [@cosandier-rimele_physiologically_2007], the brain tissue conductivity (σ) was set to 0.25 S/m (modified from the standard 0.33 S/m) to compensate for the simplifications inherent in the homogeneous model. Assuming an iEEG-MRI coregistration accuracy of 3 mm, we use the same model adjustement to prevent instabilities of the model caused by too close measurements: 

$$
\begin{align}\Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r>r_0 = 3 \text{ mm} \\ \Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r\le r_0 = 3 \text{ mm}\end{align}
$$

## Performance Evaluation Metrics

### Map to map comparison

To evaluate each method we compute the (signed) Pearson spatial correlation between the reconstructed and ground-truth activity maps at each time point:
$$
\mathcal{C}(t) = \frac{\sum_i \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{true}}(i) \cdot \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{est}}(i)}{\sigma_{\text{true}}(t) \cdot \sigma_{\text{est}}(t)}
$$

where $\mathbf s^t_{x}(i)$ is the activity at dipole $i$ and time $t$, and $\sigma_{x}(t)$ is the standard deviation of map $x$ at time $t$.

### Localization Accuracy

To evaluate localization accuracy, the source onset of the interictal spikes was defined relative to the rising phase of the discharge: this time point is a pragmatic compromise between a low probability that the source has already started propagating (favoring the discharge's onset) and an adequate signal-to-noise ratio (favoring the discharge's peak, by which point the source has typically already spread). For both the resection cohort and the simulation dataset, we used 25% of the rising phase (quarter rising phase, qrp), earlier than the 50% (half rising phase) convention of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020. The Euclidean distance was then calculated between the estimated source location and the target mask — the true seed region for the simulation dataset, or the resection volume for the resection cohort. Rather than working around voxel-grid discretization by averaging distances to several nearest voxels, we follow @carboni_linear_2022 and @wang_geometry_2026 and report the minimum Euclidean distance from the location of maximal source activity to the mask boundary, taken as 0 mm whenever that location already lies inside the mask.

### Network Concentration Index

Peak-vertex localization accuracy (above) only tests whether the single most active location falls near the resection. Epilepsy is increasingly understood as a network disorder, in which interictal discharges may arise from a distributed set of regions only partially captured by the resected tissue; testing whether reconstructed activity concentrates on the resected zone as a whole, not just at its single peak, offers a complementary view of localization. We define the Network Concentration Index (NCI): cortical vertices are ranked by absolute source activity magnitude and progressively marked active from the highest-ranked down, until a spatially contiguous cluster of area ≥ 600 mm² — the literature-established minimum synchronously active cortex needed to produce a scalp-visible interictal discharge [@grova_evaluation_2006] — first overlaps the resection. NCI is the fraction of total cortical surface area that had to be marked active for this to occur, expressed as a percentage; lower values indicate that the reconstructed network's most active regions converge more tightly onto the resected zone. As with Localization Accuracy, NCI is computed at the quarter and full rising phase for the resection cohort, using the resected volume as ground truth (Section 2.5.1). We additionally calibrate NCI against a chance level: the cortical area fraction a purely random, spatially unstructured activity map needs before any cluster — regardless of whether it overlaps the resection — reaches the 600 mm² floor, isolating the contribution of the size threshold itself from genuine localization performance.

### Channel comparison

To evaluate the accuracy of the spatial reconstruction, the projected virtual iEEG activity (Section 2.5.2) was compared against the recorded ground-truth iEEG using the (polarity-invariant) Pearson correlation between estimated and ground-truth channel activity, computed in two modes: spatially (across channels, at each timepoint) and temporally (across time, for each channel). Polarity invariance is obtained by taking the absolute value of the raw correlation ($|r|$) rather than the signed value, since an overall sign flip is an arbitrary consequence of the virtual-electrode reference convention rather than a meaningful failure mode.

For each competing method, we additionally compute a win-rate against wCSET — the fraction of channels (or time points) on which wCSET's estimate is closer to ground truth than the competitor's — summarizing pairwise performance relative to our proposed method, rather than a full all-against-all comparison across every method pair.

To test the impact of neglecting source dependences we created a simulation that is constrained by the structural connectivity. This allows us to have simulated EEG recordings with complex ground truth activity. Figure 3.1.a shows an example of an EEG recording with the key events happening. We have the peak phase, where the EEG signal is highest. At that phase, similar to what is suggested in the literature, the source has already started to propagate. Generally, it is advised to reconstruct around 50% of the rising phase (or even before if the signal to noise permits it) to properly locate the source [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020; @carboni_linear_2022]; here, the simulation's controlled SNR permits reconstructing earlier, at 25% of the rising phase (quarter rising phase, qrp). We consider as the source propagation phase everything happening after the quarter rising phase until the signal is back to noise level. We then applied source reconstruction using the five methods described in Section 2.4 (wMNE, sLORETA, dSPM, and the connectivity-informed CSET and wCSET). We did source localization to compare the accuracy of source localization. At single-trial SNR = 5, wCSET achieved significantly lower localization error than sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE (Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. wCSET, paired by region, FDR-corrected: sLORETA p < 0\.0001, effect size r = \-0\.46; dSPM p = 0\.000, r = 0\.22; wMNE p < 0\.0001, r = \-0\.94, i.e. wCSET's error was lower in every single paired region), while the difference against CSET did not reach significance (p < 0\.001, r = 0\.23). Median localization error was 5\.7 mm for wCSET, 9\.3 mm for CSET, 14\.0 mm for sLORETA, and 11\.2 mm for dSPM — all comparable in absolute terms, well within the size of a typical resection volume — whereas wMNE was a clear outlier at 61\.8 mm, consistent with its lack of noise normalization. Effect sizes therefore support a picture in which the four noise-normalized or connectivity-informed methods localize the source similarly well at this phase, with wMNE as the sole exception.

We also computed the spatial correlation time point by time point between the simulated ground truth and the reconstructions for all our source reconstruction methods. This allows us to estimate which method is best for reconstructing the source propagation. For statistical validation, we repeated the simulation 8 times for each of 100 spatially-uniform sample regions (Section 2.1.1). We then computed the median spatial correlation, together with its interquartile range across simulated runs, and plotted it over time in Figure 3. The figure shows that the spatial correlation starts at 0 (signal-to-noise ratio is null), gradually increases as the source spreads (increasing signal-to-noise ratio), then decreases again. We highlighted on the time axis the peak phase of the EEG signal and the quarter rising phase. Cluster-based permutation testing (region-paired, FDR-corrected across competitors) confirmed this pattern: wCSET's spatial correlation with the ground truth was significantly higher than sLORETA's, dSPM's, and wMNE's across nearly the entire displayed window spanning both the quarter rising phase and the peak (approximately \-12 to 116 ms; all p_corrected < 0\.001, with very large effect sizes — Cohen's dz = 4\.26, 3\.84, and 5\.98 respectively). Against CSET, wCSET and CSET both correlate much more closely with the ground truth than the other methods do, but wCSET is significantly better than CSET only in an earlier window from \-12 to 108 ms (p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = 2\.10, spanning the quarter rising phase and the very start of propagation); beyond that window the two methods were statistically indistinguishable, confirming that wCSET's advantage over CSET is concentrated near spike onset rather than sustained throughout the propagation phase.

Localization error increased for every method as SNR decreased, but the onset and severity of this degradation differed sharply across methods (Figure below, left). wMNE was affected soonest and most severely: already comparable to dSPM at the highest SNR tested (median 6\.6 mm at SNR=20), it became significantly worse than wCSET from SNR=20 down to the lowest SNR tested (region-paired cluster-permutation, p_corrected = 0\.002, Cohen's dz = 2\.15), with median error climbing to 77\.4 mm by SNR=1. sLORETA and CSET both showed a milder version of the same pattern — sLORETA staying in the 9–12 mm range from SNR=20 down to SNR=3 before climbing sharply at SNR≤2, and CSET rising more steadily from ~7 to ~17 mm over the same range before the same sharp climb — but neither reached significance against wCSET anywhere in the range tested, once corrected for the four simultaneous competitors (sLORETA's largest cluster, at SNR=20: p_corrected = 0\.003, dz = 0\.54; CSET's, at SNR=5: p_corrected = 0\.230, dz = \-0\.33). dSPM stood out as the most noise-robust standard method, remaining essentially flat (12–14 mm) from SNR=20 down to SNR=3 before rising sharply at SNR≤2; wCSET nonetheless significantly outperformed it from SNR=20 down to SNR=10 (p_corrected = 0\.005, dz = 0\.64). This advantage did not extend to the lowest SNR tested: at SNR=1, dSPM's median error (68\.7 mm) was nominally lower than wCSET's (62\.7 mm), though the difference did not itself form a significant cluster — suggesting that dSPM's noise robustness can match or exceed wCSET's own under sufficiently severe noise, even where this falls short of statistical significance.

Spatial correlation with the ground truth showed a more consistent picture (Figure below, right): wCSET significantly outperformed all four competitors at both the quarter rising phase and the peak, across the entire SNR range (region-paired cluster-permutation, all p_corrected < 0\.001; effect sizes ranging from dz = 1\.38 vs. CSET at quarter rising phase to dz = 5\.67 vs. wMNE at peak phase). Unlike localization error, this ranking held almost everywhere at low SNR too: spatial correlation declined monotonically for every method as SNR decreased (e.g. wCSET: 0\.71→\-0\.02 at quarter rising phase and 0\.76→0\.01 at peak, from SNR=20 to SNR=1), and wCSET remained the top performer across nearly the entire range — including relative to dSPM, whose noise robustness in localization error did not carry over to spatial correlation. The sole exception was the quarter rising phase at SNR=1, where correlations for every method had collapsed toward zero and wCSET's median dipped marginally (and non-significantly) below the rest; at the peak phase, wCSET stayed on top even at SNR=1.

:::{#317d0d34 .cell .markdown}
In the simulation, the true connectome is known; in practice it never is exactly. To test what happens when the wrong connectome is used, we systematically permuted the true connectome before reconstruction (Section 2.3.3) and re-evaluated localization error and spatial correlation for CSET and wCSET, this time benchmarked directly against sLORETA rather than against each other: sLORETA is connectome-agnostic, so its performance cannot be affected by connectome corruption, making it a natural floor — the degradation level at which a connectivity-informed method becomes significantly worse than sLORETA is the point past which using the (corrupted) connectome is actively counterproductive, rather than merely less helpful. dSPM remains connectome-agnostic too and is shown only as a flat, untested reference line.

wCSET's localization error remained essentially flat under permutation up to 60% (4\.4–9\.1 mm), only climbing noticeably beyond that point (11\.4 mm at 70%, 23\.1 mm at 100%). Benchmarked against sLORETA (region-paired cluster-permutation), wCSET was significantly *more* accurate across low-to-moderate degradation (0–70%, p_corrected < 0\.001, Cohen's dz = \-0\.89), and never became significantly worse than sLORETA at any degradation level tested, including full (100%) permutation. CSET showed the same early advantage over a comparable range (0–60%, p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = \-0\.69), but unlike wCSET this advantage reversed: CSET became significantly worse than sLORETA from 80% onward (p_corrected = 0\.014, dz = 0\.57) — a degradation level at which wCSET's own localization error never reached a significant deficit, even under full connectome permutation.

Spatial correlation with the ground truth showed a similar but more pronounced pattern: permutation slowly degraded wCSET's correlation (0\.52 at 0% down to 0\.09 at 100%), while CSET's own correlation stayed comparatively flat through 60% (0\.24–0\.32) before also declining sharply thereafter (0\.05 at 100%). Against sLORETA, both methods started out significantly better (region-paired cluster-permutation: CSET 0–70%, p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = \-1\.44; wCSET 0–80%, p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = \-2\.04), but only CSET's advantage reversed into a significant deficit, from 80% onward (p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = 0\.94). wCSET's correlation, by contrast, never became significantly worse than sLORETA's, even at full permutation — its apparent dip at 100% did not reach significance (p_corrected = 0\.069) — confirming that CSET's greater apparent stability up to 60% was stability at a lower level, not a genuine advantage, and that wCSET tolerates connectome corruption meaningfully better than CSET does.
:::

In clinical settings, subject-specific dMRI is often unavailable. We therefore tested whether cruder, dMRI-free connectome surrogates (Section 2.3.3) could replace the true connectome without materially harming CSET/wCSET's accuracy, comparing each surrogate directly against the original connectome for each method.

For localization error, wCSET's accuracy was statistically indistinguishable from using the true connectome for every surrogate tested (paired Wilcoxon vs. original connectome, region-paired: beltrami p < 0\.001; fused p < 0\.001; fused-bin p < 0\.001; geom-atlas p < 0\.001; geom-atlas-bin p < 0\.001 — none significant). Localization is thus similar across every surrogate for wCSET specifically, essentially insensitive to which surrogate replaces the true connectome. CSET was more sensitive to the choice of surrogate, with the beltrami and fused surrogates in particular producing a significant deficit; the full CSET breakdown is reported in the supplementary material (<!-- supp figure (CSET localization error, surrogate vs. original connectome, mirroring the wCSET panel below) -->).

For spatial correlation, differences from the original connectome were statistically significant for nearly every surrogate, but effect sizes were often small, and not all significant differences pointed the same direction. The beltrami surrogate produced the largest, most consistent drop in correlation relative to the original connectome for wCSET (p_corrected < 0\.001 at both phases, r = \-0\.68–\-0\.10) — yet even this worst case remained far more accurate than the connectome-agnostic references: wCSET's correlation with beltrami (median 0\.46 quarter rising phase, 0\.66 peak) was still roughly 3–4× higher than dSPM's (0\.11, 0\.16) or sLORETA's (0\.11, 0\.16) flagship performance with the true connectome. wCSET's pattern with the remaining surrogates was more favorable still: the fused and fused-bin surrogates were associated with significantly *higher* correlation than the original connectome (fused: p_corrected = 0\.002 quarter rising phase, p_corrected < 0\.001 peak; fused-bin: p_corrected = 0\.049 quarter rising phase, p_corrected < 0\.001 peak), and geom-atlas/geom-atlas-bin were significantly higher at quarter rising phase (p_corrected = 0\.002) but statistically indistinguishable from original at peak (p < 0\.001, p < 0\.001). CSET showed a broadly similar overall pattern of small, mostly-significant deviations from the original connectome, again largest for beltrami; the full CSET breakdown is reported in the supplementary material (<!-- supp figure (CSET spatial correlation, surrogate vs. original connectome, mirroring the wCSET panel below) -->). Together with the localization results, this indicates wCSET's accuracy is not merely insensitive to the connectome surrogate used, but for spatial correlation specifically, several cruder dMRI-free surrogates perform as well as, or nominally better than, the subject's own tractography-derived connectome.

Simulation offers a controlled testbed, but real clinical data will always differ. To verify that connectivity-informed source localization remains competitive with standard clinical methods in practice — rather than trading focal precision for network sensitivity — we evaluated localization accuracy against the resected epileptogenic zone in seizure-free patients (ILAE 1, n=26).

Alongside wMNE, sLORETA, and dSPM, we also compared against a Beltrami-eigenbasis variant of wCSET — the same Laplace-Beltrami mesh eigenmodes used as a connectome surrogate in Section 3.1.4, here run as a full 6th competitor method, in the spirit of the cortical-geometry approaches of @pang_geometric_2023, @wang_geometry_2026, and @siu_structural_2026 (Section 1). This is not a reimplementation of their exact pipelines — mesh resolution and regularization differ — but a geometry-only baseline built from machinery already validated in this work.

Peak-to-resection distance behaved similarly across most methods: wCSET's median distance (9\.6 mm) was descriptively the lowest, with Beltrami's the closest runner-up (17\.2 mm), ahead of sLORETA (18\.1 mm), CSET (18\.8 mm), and dSPM (25\.5 mm), with wMNE a clear outlier (31\.1 mm). Of the five paired comparisons against wCSET, only wMNE reached significance after FDR correction (Wilcoxon signed-rank, subject-paired: p_corrected = 0\.005, r = \-0\.54); CSET (p_corrected = 0\.077, r = \-0\.44), sLORETA (p_corrected = 0\.077, r = \-0\.48), dSPM (p_corrected = 0\.077, r = \-0\.46), and Beltrami (p_corrected = 0\.493, r = 0\.12) were not significantly different from wCSET.

The Network Concentration Index (NCI) told a different story: wCSET required markedly less of the cortex to be marked active before a cluster first touched the resection (median 1\.3% vs. 2\.0–7\.7% for the other methods) — and, contrary to our initial impression of a small effect, this difference was significant for every comparison (Wilcoxon signed-rank, subject-paired, FDR-corrected: CSET p_corrected < 0\.001, r = \-0\.92; dSPM p_corrected < 0\.001, r = \-0\.92; sLORETA p_corrected < 0\.001, r = \-0\.92; wMNE p_corrected < 0\.001, r = \-0\.77; Beltrami p_corrected = 0\.009, r = \-0\.46), all well below the 31\.6% chance level. The effect was large for CSET, sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE (|r| = 0\.77–0\.92) but visibly smaller for Beltrami (r = \-0\.46), whose median (2\.0%) came closest to wCSET's on this metric too. This indicates that the top-ranked source activity is substantially more concentrated on the true epileptogenic zone for wCSET than for any comparator method — most consistently so against CSET, sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE, and to a lesser degree against the geometry-only Beltrami variant — even though overall peak localization accuracy remains statistically comparable across methods (wMNE excepted).
