# Discussion

## Simulation take home message

The simulation begins as a focal source and spreads across the brain, its amplitude decaying with the number of graph hops from the origin. This lets the signal propagate along neighboring dipoles but also take shortcuts via long-range tracts, allowing distant regions to rise above the noise floor that pure nearest-neighbor spread could never reach on its own — a mechanism absent from neural field models. The most physiologically detailed way to enforce this would be a neural mass model [@jansen_electroencephalogram_1995], but such models become unstable at very high mass counts, either entering a critical regime or failing to share signal between masses at all [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015]. Other source-reconstruction studies therefore reduce the number of masses to around 1,000, with dipoles spaced roughly 1 cm apart [@siu_structural_2026]. At that spacing, the assumption that each dipole's effective area is much smaller than its distance to the sensors — the basis of the equivalent-dipole model that the forward solution itself depends on — begins to break down [@nunez_multi-scale_2019]. To preserve the dipole model (using ~7,600 dipoles spaced approximately 3.3 mm apart) while keeping the simulation simple enough to generate realistic EEG spikes, we adopted this patch-seeded, connectome-driven propagation model: the source itself is a spatial patch, but the propagated pattern is not necessarily one, since it can reach non-adjacent regions directly via long-range tracts rather than only spreading outward through neighbors. We do not claim that this simulation represents reality more faithfully than neural mass or neural field models, but we believe it offers insight into source-reconstruction behavior that a simple patch simulation cannot provide, while remaining tractable at high dipole counts.

A further consequence of this design is that the EEG signal's peak systematically lags the true onset of the underlying source: although the simulated source itself is strongest at onset, propagation delay means that by the time the *scalp* signal reaches its own peak, the source has already spread considerably — consistent with the broader clinical literature on interictal discharge propagation [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020; @carboni_linear_2022]. This is precisely why the field favors an earlier point in the rising phase over the peak for source localization: at that point the signal is already detectable, but activity remains largely concentrated near the true onset, with only limited spread having occurred. Here, the simulation's controlled SNR let us reconstruct even earlier than the field's typical 50% convention, at 25% of the rising phase (quarter rising phase, qrp).

### Localization versus spread

Most simulation-based source-reconstruction studies focus on localization and report both location and spatial extent. At the quarter rising phase, the source is still relatively focal and largely independent from the rest of the cortex. Methods such as sLORETA and dSPM were designed to optimize localization accuracy but do not explicitly address extent; more recent methods instead prioritize extent and typically report improved results over these classical baselines. In this study, wCSET's localization error at the quarter rising phase was significantly lower than sLORETA's, dSPM's, and wMNE's, but its advantage over CSET — the other connectivity-informed method — did not reach significance (p_corrected < 0\.001, r = 0\.23; Section 3.1.1). We do not report extent using the precision/recall-style metrics common in the literature [@bradley_evaluation_2016], since thresholding the reconstructed activity into a binary "active" mask would require an arbitrary and difficult-to-justify cutoff. Instead we measure spatial correlation with the ground truth, and the higher correlation already visible for wCSET and CSET at the quarter rising phase hints at a genuine improvement in extent, consistent with reports from similar connectivity- and geometry-informed methods [@wang_geometry_2026; @siu_structural_2026]. This improvement can be explained by the fact that connectivity matrices include local, neighboring connections that help define spatially coherent patches of activity.

That said, connectivity-informed source reconstruction offers more than an improvement in source extent: because it is constrained by the brain's actual connections, it also addresses the spread problem directly. We show that spatial correlation improves markedly as the signal spreads toward the EEG peak, indicating that these methods can potentially reconstruct the brain's dynamics well beyond the initial stimulus — or, in the clinical case, beyond the onset of an interictal epileptiform discharge. Irrespective of method, correlation increases toward the peak phase; part of this is simply the higher signal-to-noise ratio at that point, which is also why sLORETA's correlation rises over the same window. The much larger gain observed for wCSET and CSET, however, is better explained by the connectome-spectrum literature: as activity spreads across the cortex, its representation becomes increasingly compact in the connectome-harmonic domain, with this compactness itself tracking the signal's power [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. In other words, as the source spreads, it becomes progressively better described by a small number of graph harmonics — exactly the representation wCSET and CSET are built around — which explains their disproportionate gain in correlation as the peak phase approaches. What matters for comparing methods, then, is not that correlation rises for everyone as SNR improves, but the widening gap between connectivity-informed and connectivity-agnostic methods over that same window.

### Robustness to inaccuracies

To verify that this improvement is not merely a noise-free artifact, we repeated source reconstruction across a range of single-trial SNRs and connectome degradation levels (Section 3.1.2). Localization error increased for every method as SNR decreased, but the point at which each method broke down differed substantially: wMNE degraded soonest and most severely, already comparable to dSPM at the highest SNR tested (median 6\.6 mm at SNR=20) before rising well above sLORETA's and CSET's error at lower SNR, while sLORETA and CSET held up longer before degrading sharply at the lowest SNRs tested. dSPM was the most noise-robust of the standard methods, remaining essentially flat across most of the range tested — consistent with prior reports that dSPM's noise normalization improves on unnormalized minimum-norm estimates under noise [@dale_dynamic_2000] — and it ultimately overtook wCSET at the most extreme noise level tested (SNR=1: median 68\.7 mm for dSPM vs. 62\.7 mm for wCSET). Spatial correlation degraded more gradually for every method, without a comparable sharp breakdown point, and wCSET remained the top performer across the entire SNR range tested, including relative to dSPM.

One limitation of this analysis is that SNR was calibrated on the single trial, before averaging 20 epochs into the evoked response used for reconstruction; since averaging itself raises the effective SNR of the signal that is actually reconstructed, the single-trial value we vary does not equal the SNR of the reconstructed evoked response. We did not additionally vary the number of averaged epochs, so how the two factors trade off against one another remains untested.

Degrading the connectome produced a single, monotonic decline in performance for both methods, rather than the two-phase pattern we initially suspected. Under permutation, CSET's spatial correlation stayed comparatively flat (0\.24–0\.32) through 60% degradation (Section 3.1.3), which first suggested that the harmonics driving reconstruction accuracy might simply be the most robust ones, irrespective of graph frequency. We initially attempted to encode this directly, weighting harmonics with a U-shaped profile based on @sipes_integrative_2024's finding that harmonic robustness to connectome perturbation follows the gap-spectrum (the difference between consecutive eigenvalues), favoring so-called integrative harmonics (the low-frequency end of the spectrum) and segregative harmonics (the high-frequency end) over the intermediate, degenerate ones. In practice, however, retaining the high-frequency end of this U introduced visible reconstruction artifacts, likely a consequence of how sparse high-frequency harmonics are. We therefore aligned with the broader literature and instead adopted an exponential decay, weighting only the low-frequency end of the spectrum — the choice that became wCSET — which improved on CSET's spatial correlation with the ground truth: benchmarked directly against the connectome-agnostic sLORETA baseline (which cannot itself be affected by connectome corruption), CSET's correlation advantage reversed into a significant deficit from 80% permutation onward, while wCSET's held significant through 80% and only became statistically indistinguishable from sLORETA at full permutation (region-paired cluster-permutation vs. sLORETA; Section 3.1.3). Localization error showed essentially the same qualitative pattern: CSET's own early advantage over sLORETA (significant through 60% permutation) likewise reversed into a significant deficit from 80% permutation onward, while wCSET's advantage — significant through 70% — never reversed into a significant deficit at any degradation level tested, including full permutation. On both metrics, the absolute gap between wCSET and CSET narrowed steadily as degradation increased, and both converged toward the connectome-agnostic sLORETA/dSPM baselines by full permutation — consistent with a fully permuted connectome carrying essentially no genuine structural information at that point, leaving both methods in much the same position as sLORETA and dSPM, which never used the connectome at all. wCSET's median localization error at full permutation was nonetheless numerically higher than sLORETA's and dSPM's (23\.1 mm vs. 14\.0 and 11\.2 mm respectively) without this gap reaching significance — a discrepancy we do not yet fully understand. This indicates that our methods tolerate substantial rewiring while still benefiting from whatever structure remains, which is encouraging given the well-documented limitations of tractography, which produces substantially more false-positive than true-positive white matter bundles [@maier-hein_challenge_2017], and it further suggests that even fairly crude connectome surrogates should support reasonable reconstruction accuracy.

### Using surrogates

We tested several ways to build a connectome surrogate for settings where subject-specific dMRI is unavailable: extrapolating a dipole-level connectome from a published atlas, relying purely on cortical geometry via our own local-connectivity rule, and the increasingly popular Laplace-Beltrami operator. We also tested whether the edge weights themselves matter, by comparing each weighted surrogate against its binarized (presence/absence) counterpart. For localization error, wCSET performed similarly across every surrogate, statistically indistinguishable from using the true connectome in every case (Section 3.1.4); CSET was more sensitive, differing significantly from the true connectome specifically with the Beltrami and fused surrogates. For spatial correlation, the Beltrami surrogate produced the largest, most consistent drop relative to the true connectome for both methods — yet even in this worst case, wCSET's correlation using Beltrami remained several times higher than dSPM's or sLORETA's using the true connectome. The binarized and weighted versions of the fused and geometry-only surrogates performed very similarly to one another, suggesting that the precise edge weights contribute comparatively little beyond the surrogate's topology. We used the fused surrogate for the clinical data, but no surrogate was a clear overall winner.

Overall, these results suggest that the Beltrami operator — Wang and colleagues' approach [@wang_geometry_2026] — performs nearly as well as the true connectome, consistent with the ongoing debate over whether cortical geometry or structural connectivity better explains functional brain activity [@pang_geometric_2023]. This comparison, however, arguably disadvantages the Beltrami operator by construction, since we treat the true dMRI-derived connectome as ground truth throughout. Under realistic noise, and in a real rather than simulated brain, it is plausible that the Beltrami operator would perform just as well or better, if fast neural information genuinely travels preferentially across the cortical sheet rather than along white matter tracts — a hypothesis with growing support from work showing that cortical geometry alone constrains a substantial share of observed brain function and dynamics [@pang_geometric_2023].

A plausible mathematical explanation for why these surrogates perform almost as well as the real connectome is that wCSET's exponential weighting emphasizes only a small number of low-frequency graph harmonics. These harmonics correspond to coarse, large-scale structure — such as the hemispheric and lobar organization of the cortex — that is broadly shared across very different connectome constructions (tractography-derived, atlas-derived, or purely geometric), even when their fine-grained, high-frequency detail differs substantially. If so, only the small number of harmonics that most constructions happen to agree on ever really matter for reconstruction, which would also explain why the exact edge weights contribute so little beyond topology alone.

### Limitations

These simulations let us probe source-reconstruction behavior under fully known ground truth, but they necessarily idealize several aspects of real recordings: known conductivities save for the deliberate forward-model mismatch (Section 2.3.2), a single representative subject, and propagation and noise models that, while physiologically motivated, remain simplified approximations of real cortical dynamics. Some of these modelling assumptions may not hold in real brains, which is precisely why the remainder of this Discussion turns to clinical data, where the same methods are evaluated against ground truths — resection outcome and simultaneous intracranial recordings — that carry their own, different limitations, but are not simulated.

## Epilepsy with Resected Ground Truth

We used this dataset to test source localization against a widely accepted clinical benchmark and to establish a point of comparison with existing approaches. The simulation suggested that connectivity information provides little improvement in single-source localization accuracy relative to CSET specifically (p_corrected < 0\.001, r = 0\.23), and this dataset, evaluated with an approach similar to the prior literature, confirms that picture: peak-to-resection distance did not differ significantly across methods (Section 3.2.1). This evaluation has two notable limitations. First, we lack a precise delineation of the epileptogenic zone, only the coarser resected volume as a proxy. Second, localization accuracy here is considerably worse than in the simulation: given the resection volume's typical size, a source localized with the accuracy seen in simulation should fall inside it essentially every time, yet clinical reconstructions instead show a broad, blurred pattern of activity under sLORETA and a more clearly delineated one under wCSET. This discrepancy may reflect an underestimate of physiological noise in our simulations, or the possibility that, by the 50% rising phase, the clinical interictal discharge has already spread considerably.

This observation motivated a complementary metric: because reconstructions at the 50% rising phase already show multiple discrete regions of activity — suggesting either that the spike has spread substantially by that point, or that it never depended on a single region to begin with — we searched for the smallest fraction of the cortex that must be marked active before a cluster first touches the resection. This metric shows that all methods reach the resection zone well before chance level, indicating that the true focus is reconstructed correctly but missed by metrics that consider only the single peak vertex. This is consistent with genuine spread, but also with the now well-established view that epilepsy is fundamentally a network phenomenon rather than a single-generator disease [@spencer_neural_2002; @kramer_epilepsy_2012], in which several regions jointly sustain a positive-feedback loop that generates the interictal discharge; removing any single node of that loop could relieve symptoms even without resecting the point of maximal reconstructed activity. This cluster-based view could in principle help delineate such networks, but doing so is beyond the scope of the present work.

### Epilepsy with intracranial electrode

Intracranial electrodes measure the true electrical activity inside the brain, but they cover only a small fraction of it and record electrical potential rather than dipole current directly. Comparing them to source reconstructions therefore requires an additional, error-prone step: projecting reconstructed sources onto the intracranial channel locations. We adopted Grova's approach for this projection (Section 2.5.2) and defined our own comparison metrics. Grova's original method focuses mainly on the spike peak, considering at most the five time points immediately surrounding it — given their reported 1200 Hz MEG/EEG sampling rate, a window of approximately 3.3 ms. To test whether wCSET improves reconstruction not only at the spike itself but also during its spread, as our simulations predict, we extended this window using the GFP-threshold spike window described in Section 2.2.1: the continuous interval around the peak over which global field power remains above a fixed number of standard deviations of the pre-spike baseline, rather than a fixed five-sample neighborhood. We also excluded Grova's measure of spurious activity, since it presupposes that activity elsewhere in the brain is necessarily an artifact — an assumption at odds with the premise that spike-related activity can genuinely be distributed.

Two of the four subjects have deep sources: despite clear evidence of the spike in the intracranial recording, no corresponding spike is visible on the scalp EEG. Unsurprisingly, no method reconstructs the intracranial channels well in these two subjects, a limitation also reported in Grova's own work. Of the two subjects with a visible EEG spike, one shows only a small difference between methods, while the other shows a marked advantage for wCSET, reflected in significantly higher spatial correlation with the true intracranial recording; temporal correlation was not significantly higher for that subject (Section 3.3.1). Within each subject, we accounted for the fact that all channels or timepoints being compared originate from the same spike and the same subject by correcting the effective sample size for their autocorrelation, rather than treating each channel or timepoint as an independent observation; this does not, however, address the separate limitation that only four subjects are available in total, which precluded any statistical test across independent subjects. We also did not adopt Grova's own patch-wise reconstruction approach; in exchange, our data offer a genuine advantage over Grova's, in that scalp EEG and intracranial recordings were acquired simultaneously, rather than separately as in Grova's work, where the two modalities could not be recorded together for MEG-specific reasons.

A further limitation of the present framework is its reliance on a cortically constrained source model. Any EEG activity is projected onto the cortical surface even when it may have originated from deeper structures, which is common in epilepsy; the reconstruction can then conserve the correct overall energy while still misplacing it on the cortex, distorting the resulting virtual intracranial signal at deeper channels. Modelling deeper sources would require an orientation-free source model, which would in turn require the connectivity structure to encode each source's preferred orientation — a capability that does not yet exist, to our knowledge. One possible route forward would be to inform voxel orientations directly from tractography and constrain sources accordingly, but we leave this for future work. As it stands, connectivity-informed source reconstruction remains limited to fixed source orientations.

# Conclusion

This work introduced weighted CSET (wCSET), a connectivity-informed source reconstruction method that replaces CSET's L1 sparsity prior in the connectome spectrum with a smooth, exponentially weighted L2 prior, and evaluated it alongside standard, connectivity-agnostic methods across three complementary studies designed to probe source reconstruction beyond simple localization.

In simulation, wCSET matched or improved on standard methods for locating a source's onset, but its real advantage emerged in reconstructing how that activity subsequently spreads: spatial correlation with the ground truth improved substantially as the signal propagated, a gain attributable to the increasing compactness of spreading activity in the connectome-harmonic domain. This advantage proved robust to substantial noise and to considerable inaccuracy in the connectome itself, including edge rearrangement and the use of crude, dMRI-free connectome surrogates — though we also identified real limits to this robustness: at the most extreme noise levels tested, dSPM's localization accuracy exceeded wCSET's, and outright removal of connectome edges degraded localization far more severely than it degraded spatial correlation.

In a large clinical cohort with resection outcome as ground truth, wCSET preserved localization accuracy comparable to established clinical algorithms, while a cluster-based extent metric showed its reconstructed activity converging on the resected zone with markedly less of the cortex marked active than any comparator method — evidence that the gain in network sensitivity does not come at the cost of focal precision. Finally, in a small cohort with simultaneous EEG and intracranial recordings, wCSET reproduced the true intracranial activity pattern more closely than standard methods in at least one subject, directly supporting the central premise that connectivity-informed reconstruction can capture distributed neural dynamics beyond what point-localization benchmarks can measure, though the small number of subjects available limits how far this specific result can be generalized.

Together, these studies support wCSET as a principled, clinically viable step beyond localization-only source imaging, and more broadly demonstrate the value of evaluating source reconstruction against a source's full, distributed activity pattern rather than its location alone. We see two natural directions for future work: extending the model beyond fixed cortical source orientations so that deeper, epilepsy-relevant sources can be represented directly, and validating these findings in larger, independent clinical cohorts with simultaneous intracranial recordings.
